title: One Classroom Management Strategy For Every Student very-student/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Prompted by an email from a struggling teacher, Linsin lays out his counterintuitive recommendation for handling chronically disruptive students: give them no more attention, discussion, or special handling than any other student. He argues that the common instinct to devote extra lectures, scoldings, warnings, counseling sessions, and even praise to troublesome students backfires, since it signals to those students that they are fundamentally different and unable to control themselves, damaging their self-esteem and reinforcing a troublemaker identity that persists year after year. His proposed alternative is to apply the classroom management plan to disruptive students exactly as it applies to everyone else -- delivering the same consequences, offering the same ordinary praise, and refusing to discuss or dwell on behavior issues beyond enforcing the plan. He acknowledges this approach may produce a difficult transition period of a week or two, with increased time-outs and more dramatic acting out, before behavior improves. He closes by arguing that disruptive students actually respond well to this style precisely because it is fair, consistent, and free of the emotional charge that typically surrounds their interactions with teachers.
points: Giving chronically disruptive students extra attention, discussion, or special handling is argued to reinforce their unwanted behavior rather than reduce it.
Excess attention communicates to struggling students that they are fundamentally different and unable to control themselves, damaging self-esteem over time.
The recommended strategy is to treat disruptive students exactly like every other student -- same consequences, same praise, no special lectures or counseling sessions.
Teachers should expect a difficult one-to-two week transition period, with increased time-outs and more dramatic behavior, before the strategy shows results.
Disruptive students reportedly respond well to this consistent, unemotional approach because it removes tension and confusion from their relationship with the teacher.
quotes: Some of my classroom management solutions run counter to what many teachers are doing, and in the case of students who repeatedly disrupt the classroom, this is also true. For example, I don’t speak more often to misbehaving-prone students or give them more attention than I would any other student.
Giving more attention to troublesome students increases the likelihood that their unwanted behavior will continue. Yet, in my experience, this seems to be the preferred method.

When you attend to poorly behaved students more often, you’re communicating to them in a subtle but clear way that they’re different, that they don’t have what it takes to control themselves like other students.
So what is the solution? Ignore the behavior and hope it goes away? Tiptoe around the student(s) and hope they aren’t too disruptive? No, the solution is to treat them just like everyone else.
When you begin using this strategy, the first couple of weeks or so may be tough. One or more of your students may be in time-out a lot, they may act out more than usual and more dramatically.

In my experience, those students with disruptive tendencies love this style of classroom management. It’s fair, and because it isn’t arbitrary or based on personal feelings, it completely removes tension between the student and his or her teacher.
